title: WWDC23: Animate with springs | Apple
summary: Jacob from Apple explains why springs are the default animation across iOS: they are the only kind that keeps both position AND velocity continuous, so motion can pick up a finger's speed at the end of a gesture and change course mid-flight without a jolt. He reduces springs to two designer-friendly parameters (duration and bounce), shows the three shapes (bouncy, smooth, flattened) and ends with concrete tuning guidance: pick duration first, then bounce, default to 0, stay under about 0.4.

insights.insight: Animation exists first for continuity: an object that vanishes in one place and appears in another feels jarring and confusing. But continuous position is not enough; a sudden change of SPEED (motion that starts or stops at full velocity) also feels wrong. Goal: continuous position and continuous velocity.
insights.quote: one goal we have is to make our animations have continuous position and velocity
insights.visual: Ease-in-out demo: the white knob next to its position-over-time chart, an S-curve with no corners at either end.

insights.insight: Linear timing has hard corners: velocity jumps at start and end, a non-physical motion that feels out of place for anything that moves. Keep linear only for special cases such as a continuously spinning loader.
insights.visual: 'Linear' slide: the position chart is a straight diagonal with sharp corners where it meets the start and end lines, the playhead mid-way.

insights.insight: Gesture handoff is where curves fail. When the user throws an element and lets go, an ease-in-out curve cannot accept the finger's speed, so the object jerks to a halt and then restarts. A spring can start with any initial velocity, so the animation continues seamlessly from the gesture (in 1D and 2D drags).
insights.quote: our animation picks up right where the gesture ends
insights.visual: A hand flicks the round knob across an iPad screen; the knob is mid-flight toward its resting spot after the finger has released.

insights.insight: Springs end the way real objects do: they settle gradually with no single moment where they are abruptly 'done', which is why even zero-bounce springs read as natural. A spring is not the same as 'bouncy'; non-bouncy springs are used all over iOS.
insights.visual: 'Spring' slide: the chart rises quickly then eases into a long flat tail toward the target line; an orange arrow marks the starting velocity.

insights.insight: Choreography from staggered springs: properties do NOT need to start and stop together. The iOS app-launch is several springs with different start and end times (window grows from the icon, home screen blurs and recedes, content settles) that together read as one natural move. Slowed down, the layers are clearly offset.
insights.quote: different start times, and different end times come together
insights.visual: Slowed-down app launch: the Settings window is half-grown out of its icon position while the home-screen widgets and icons behind it are blurred and pushed back.

insights.insight: Configure springs with two perceptual parameters instead of mass/stiffness/damping: duration (pacing) and bounce (character, -100% to 100%). Bounce > 0 overshoots (bouncy), 0 is a smooth curve with a long tail, < 0 is flatter (useful for scroll-like decay).
insights.visual: Three charts side by side labelled Bouncy (100% > bounce > 0%, overshoot then settle), Smooth (bounce = 0%) and Flattened (0% > bounce > -100%).

insights.insight: Interruptible motion: if a new target arrives while an animation is still running (the user taps again), a spring takes its current velocity as the starting velocity toward the new destination, so redirection is smooth instead of snapping or restarting from zero.
insights.visual: The knob on the iPad mid-way to a new spot the finger just tapped, with a faint ghost knob marking its target, under a deliberately slow spring.

insights.insight: Tuning recipe: first find the duration that gives the pacing you like, then add bounce for character. 0 = smooth general-purpose default; ~0.15 = brisk, not visibly bouncy; ~0.3 = noticeably bouncy, good for playful or end-of-gesture moments; above ~0.4 risks feeling exaggerated for UI. Keep values consistent with the app's personality (serious vs playful, relaxed vs fast).
insights.quote: be cautious about using values higher than around 0.4
insights.visual: Code 'withAnimation(.spring(duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.6))' with an orange warning badge, flagging a too-bouncy setting.

apply_to_wael: Use springs, not linear or fixed ease curves, for every move in the first-launch flow (Framer Motion / motion 'type: spring' with visualDuration + bounce, or CSS linear() spring approximations): step panels and the island camera with bounce 0 (~0.5-0.6 s), Wael's hops and the reward/result pop with bounce ~0.25-0.3, never above 0.4.

Make the transitions interruptible: if the student taps 'next' or a choice while the camera or Wael is still moving, retarget from the current position and velocity instead of finishing the old animation or jumping (springs in JS keep velocity; CSS transitions on transform also retarget).

Copy the app-launch choreography for splash -> welcome and subject -> game: the foreground card grows from the tapped badge while the 3D town behind blurs, dims and scales back to ~0.9, each on its own slightly offset spring, so it reads as one continuous move rather than a page swap.

If the town map or level picker is draggable/swipeable, hand the finger's release velocity to the spring so the map glides and settles instead of stopping dead, and reverse the camera move when the gesture is cancelled.
